Reviewing the Design File

Reviewing the Design File

Before any code gets written, the design itself gets reviewed: layers, components, font licenses, and asset exports. Missing states (hover, empty cart, out-of-stock) and mobile variants get flagged here. A well-organized Figma file makes everything downstream faster; a messy one creates back-and-forth revisions that slow the whole process down.

Converting Sections into Liquid

Each frame in the Figma file — hero banner, product grid, footer — becomes its own Liquid section. This isn’t a one-to-one copy-paste. It’s rebuilt as reusable, structured code that works within Shopify’s Online Store 2.0 architecture, meaning merchants can later rearrange or reuse these sections without needing a developer for every small change.

Applying Styles and Dynamic Content

Spacing, colors, and typography from the design get recreated in code. Then static placeholders get replaced with real Shopify data: product titles, prices, images, collections, pulled dynamically so the page displays correctly no matter which product someone’s viewing.

Building Responsive Design

With over half of ecommerce traffic happening on mobile, every section gets tested and adjusted across breakpoints, not just resized, but checked for text readability, image scaling, and how layouts actually behave on smaller screens. A design that looks perfect on desktop and breaks on mobile isn’t finished yet.

Optimizing for Performance

Images get compressed, unused CSS gets removed, and lazy loading gets applied to reduce load time. This step matters more than it might seem, since even a well-designed store will lose sales if it loads slowly. Core Web Vitals like LCP and CLS get tuned specifically for this.

QA and Cross-Browser Testing

Every section gets tested across major browsers and devices, checking layout, interactions, forms, and especially the cart and checkout flow. This is the step most likely to get rushed, and it’s also where small issues, broken hover states, mismatched fonts, and spacing bugs quietly undermine an otherwise well-built store.

Where Conversion Comes In

A pixel-perfect design isn’t the same as a high-converting one. Throughout this process, good developers watch for anything that could create friction: slow-loading images, confusing mobile navigation, checkout steps that don’t match the polish of the rest of the store. The build should preserve the design’s intent while actively supporting the goal behind it: getting visitors to buy.

Why the Workflow Matters

Skipping steps, especially QA or performance optimization, is how a beautiful design turns into a store that looks right but underperforms. A structured Shopify design-to-development workflow protects against that: it’s not just about matching pixels; it’s about making sure the finished store actually works the way the design intended.

The Bottom Line

A successful Figma-to-Shopify build looks exactly like the design and performs even better. That only happens with a clear process, from design review through QA, not by skipping straight from mockup to launch.

Have a Figma file ready and want to see it built right?
